vignette.stem: A 58-year-old man with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus presents to the emergency department with 45 minutes of substernal chest pressure radiating to his left arm, associated with diaphoresis and nausea. Vital signs: BP 148/90 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air. Physical examination reveals no jugular venous distension, clear lung fields bilaterally, and a regular heart rhythm without murmurs or rubs. An ECG and troponin have been ordered but results are not yet available.
vignette.question: Based on the information available, which is the most appropriate immediate next step in management?

options.B: Activate the cardiac catheterization laboratory for primary percutaneous coronary intervention
options.C: Initiate anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin and dual antiplatelet therapy
options.D: Perform urgent coronary artery bypass grafting

vignette.rationale: The critical missing information is the ECG result and the initial troponin value, both of which are required to classify the type of acute coronary syndrome (if any) and to determine the appropriate management pathway. Without these data, none of the four management options can be justified. Option A (fibrinolytic therapy) is indicated only for ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) when primary PCI is unavailable or door-to-balloon time cannot be achieved within guideline-recommended windows; it requires ECG confirmation of ST-elevation or new LBBB and is contraindicated in many settings — none of which can be assessed without the ECG. Option B (primary PCI activation) is the preferred reperfusion strategy for STEMI, but requires ECG documentation of ST-elevation or new LBBB meeting STEMI criteria; activating the catheterization laboratory without ECG confirmation is not guideline-supported and exposes the patient to unnecessary procedural risk if no STEMI is present. Option C (anticoagulation plus dual antiplatelet therapy) is the standard initial treatment for NSTEMI or unstable angina, but these diagnoses require at minimum an ECG showing ischemic changes without ST-elevation and/or a positive troponin; initiating full antithrombotic therapy before the ECG and troponin are available risks harm (e.g., bleeding) if the presentation is non-ACS. Option D (urgent CABG) is reserved for specific high-risk anatomic findings identified on coronary angiography (e.g., left main or complex multivessel disease) and is never an immediate first step without diagnostic imaging and angiographic data. The correct response is to recognize that the ECG and troponin results are indispensable before any of these interventions can be chosen.
sources: O'Gara PT et al. 2013 ACCF/AHA Guideline for the Management of ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction. Circulation 2013;127:e362-e425.
